opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting shifts happening right now. Early on, a lot of the progress came from carefully curated data: expert annotators, labeled datasets, people writing high-quality demonstrations. That was really important for getting models to a baseline where they're useful and behave reasonably.

But curated supervision doesn't scale the way usage does. Once you have millions of people using these systems every day, the signal coming from ordinary interactions starts to dwarf what any team of annotators can produce. Did the person accept the answer? Did they rephrase the question? Did they edit the code the model wrote? That's an enormous amount of real-world feedback about what's actually useful, not just what an annotator thought was a good answer in isolation.

So I see the balance moving toward user feedback, but with a couple of important caveats. First, that feedback is noisy and can be gamed, so you still need curated, high-trust data to anchor things, especially for safety, reasoning, and specialized domains where an average user can't easily judge correctness. Second, and this is the part I care a lot about, there's the question of who owns that feedback and who benefits from it. Right now, users generate this incredibly valuable training signal and it mostly flows into a few centralized companies. They don't get attribution, compensation, or real say over how it's used.

I think the future looks more like a system where people contribute data and feedback intentionally, with clear consent, maybe get rewarded for it, and where you can track provenance: which contributions actually improved the model. That aligns incentives much better. You get higher-quality signal because people are motivated to give good feedback, and the models end up reflecting the interests of the people using them rather than just whoever controls the platform.

So: curated supervision for the foundation and the guardrails, user feedback increasingly for the long tail of real-world usefulness, and hopefully infrastructure that makes that feedback loop fair and transparent.

r001.rationale: The response says curated supervision is useful for the foundation and guardrails, while user feedback should increasingly guide real-world usefulness. It does not say trained evaluators are preferable for tuning conversational feel or personality.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the shift is already underway, and it's going to accelerate. Early on, with RLHF and the first instruction-tuned models, you really needed curated supervision. You hired annotators, you wrote detailed rubrics, you had people rank responses carefully. That was necessary because the models were not good enough to extract signal from noisy data. But that approach has a ceiling. It's expensive, it's slow, and fundamentally the annotators are a small group of people imposing their preferences on everyone else.

What actually matters is whether the model is useful to the specific person using it. And the richest signal for that is what happens after the model responds. Did the user accept the suggestion? Did they edit it? Did they come back and ask the same thing a different way? Did they abandon the task? That's not something you can get from a contractor in a labeling queue. That's ordinary feedback from real usage, and there is orders of magnitude more of it.

The challenge is that this feedback is implicit, it's noisy, and it's often misaligned with what you actually want. If you just optimize for engagement, you get the same failure modes we saw with social media. So I don't think curated supervision disappears. I think its role changes. Instead of being the primary training signal, it becomes the thing that defines the objective, the constraints, the guardrails, and then the volume comes from users.

And there's another dimension I care about a lot, which is who owns that feedback. Right now every interaction you have with a model is captured by whoever runs the model, and they use it to improve their product. The user gets nothing back except a slightly better model later, maybe. I think the direction we need to go is where users actually own their data and their contributions, and they can choose to give it to models that align with them, and there's some accountability and even compensation for that. If you get that right, you can also get much higher quality feedback, because people participate deliberately instead of just being observed.

So to answer the question directly: the balance tips strongly toward user feedback, but the interesting work is in building the systems that make that feedback trustworthy and make the models accountable to the people providing it.

r001.rationale: The response favors ordinary user feedback as the main training signal and does not say trained evaluators are preferable for tuning conversational feel or personality.

astra-6.text:
I think the balance shifts toward learning from actual usage, but curated supervision still plays an important role. It gives the model a starting point: examples of what a useful answer looks like and what you want the system to do.

Once people start using it, you get a much broader set of situations than a team could curate ahead of time. A user might correct an answer, ask the question again, or take the output and change it. Those interactions can tell you where the model is falling short.

The challenge is that feedback is ambiguous. If someone stops responding, did they get what they needed, or did they give up? And an answer that people like isn't necessarily correct. So I see this as a loop: use real interactions to discover problems, then use more deliberate supervision and evaluation to make sure you're actually improving the system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curated supervision and ordinary user feedback in general, but it does not say trained evaluators are preferable for tuning conversational feel or personality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the balance shifts as the model becomes more useful. Early on, you need curated examples to teach it what a good response looks like. But once people are using it, they expose a much broader range of problems than a team can anticipate when building a dataset.

The challenge is that user feedback is noisy. If somebody stops a conversation, did they get what they needed, or did they give up? And what people prefer in the moment isn’t always what’s correct. So I see these as complementary: user feedback helps you discover where the model falls short, and curated supervision helps you turn those observations into a reliable learning signal.

r001.rationale: The response says curated supervision and user feedback are complementary, but does not say trained evaluators’ feedback is preferable for tuning conversational feel or personality.
